name: New Jersey Performing Arts Center
label: NJPAC
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Military Park' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Military Park' (way/76554678): middle (401 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/75687568: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'New Jersey Performing Arts Center' (154 m across).
notes: Newark's main performing arts venue on Center Street.

text.description:
The New Jersey Performing Arts Center, usually called NJPAC, is one of the largest performing arts centres in the United States and a landmark of Downtown Newark. It opened in October 1997 on the site of the former Military Park Hotel. It is the home of the New Jersey Symphony Orchestra. The architect, Barton Myers, chose brick, exposed steel and glass to echo Newark's industrial past, and the result looks like a working part of the city rather than a grand monument.

That mix of materials is why it photographs well. From Military Park you see the facade across Park Place, with the park's trees in the foreground and the downtown high-rises behind. The trees give you a natural frame and the tall buildings show where the centre sits in the city. NJPAC is not the only building in view from here, so decide whether you want a wide scene of the whole street or a tighter shot of the centre alone.

Stand on the park side facing Park Place and let the facade fill the middle of the picture. Wait for a gap in the traffic and passers-by if you want a clean frame. Keep the phone level so the vertical lines of the building stay straight. If you want a second angle, cross the street and photograph the entrance and the brickwork up close.
text.geographic_location: NJPAC is in Downtown Newark, in the city's cultural district around Military Park and Washington Park. It stands just west of the Passaic River waterfront, with the Prudential Center a little to the south.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot; head for Military Park in Downtown Newark. Stand on the side of the park facing Park Place. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the facade and the street in one frame. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if trees or people block the view and you want to fit in more of the buildings. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for brick and glass details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Military Park (park side facing Park Place, where NJPAC sits across the street). NJPAC's facade across Park Place, framed by the park's trees and the downtown high-rises around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the building up with the vertical lines so it does not lean. Use a tree branch or trunk at the edge of the picture as a frame. Keep the facade in the middle of the frame and let the high-rises fill the background. For a second angle, cross Park Place and shoot the entrance from the pavement.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky is bright, so the brick keeps its colour. If the scene is wider than your screen, try panorama mode and hold the phone steady as you sweep.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight with soft, even light gives the best colour on the brick. Around dusk, when the building's lights come on, try night mode and hold the phone still.

text.access_note: Military Park is a public park; check its current state before you go, and check the official NJPAC site before you go if you want to see inside.

name: Sports Illustrated Stadium
label: Sports Illustrated Sta
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'East Newark Riverfront Park' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'East Newark Riverfront Park' (way/1385911079): middle (343 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/75692796: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Sports Illustrated Stadium' (267 m across).
notes: Soccer stadium across the Passaic River in Harrison.

text.description:
Sports Illustrated Stadium is a football (soccer) ground on the Passaic River waterfront, home to the New York Red Bulls and Gotham FC. It opened in 2010 as Red Bull Arena and took its current name in December 2024. The shape is what you will want to photograph. A curved, partly translucent fabric roof wraps around the whole stadium, and about 60 feet (18 m) of it lets daylight through. It holds 25,000 seats, and the roof covers every one of them.

The stadium is in Harrison, across the river from Newark, so the map's stand-here point is not at the ground itself. It is at East Newark Riverfront Park, a riverside green space with walking paths, at the corner of Clay St and Passaic Ave. From here the stadium lies to the south-east, a little over two kilometres away. This is a calm place to photograph the open water of the Passaic and the skyline beyond. Whether the stadium roof shows from the park is not confirmed, so have a look on the ground. If it does, it will be small and distant.

For a closer shot of the roof, the stadium exterior is the alternative. One guide says new housing now blocks the clear view seen in older photos, so expect a narrower angle than you may have seen online. Frame the roof against the sky, keep the phone level, and let the curve do the work.
text.geographic_location: The stadium is in the Riverbend District of Harrison, on the east bank of the Passaic River, directly across the water from Newark.
text.directions_text: No public transport is listed for this spot, so use a map app on your phone to find the route to the East Newark riverside area, and look for the corner of Clay St and Passaic Ave. The stadium is a little over two kilometres to the south-east of the park. Check the walking route on your phone's map. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the river and sky. Use the default lens (1x) for a balanced view of the water and skyline. If the stadium roof is visible, try the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick it out.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in East Newark Riverfront Park (Clay St and Passaic Ave, riverside edge). Open waterfront on the Passaic River, a quieter alternative to the stadium exterior; the stadium's visibility from here is not confirmed by the sources. From here you can photograph the open waterfront on the Passaic. The stadium lies to the south-east, so look that way for its roof and see whether it shows between the buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Use the gridlines and place the river along the lower third, with sky above. If the stadium is visible, put its curved roof on one of the grid intersections and zoom in rather than crop later. For a closer view of the stadium exterior, go to the stadium itself and shoot the curved, translucent roof from further back, where the housing allows.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the water or the roof to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Use the telephoto at 2x or 3x for distance shots and hold the phone against a railing or your body to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the water. On match days the area around the stadium gets busy, so check the fixture list before you pick a time.

text.access_note: The park is a public riverside space, but check the official site before you go for stadium access, especially on match days.
claims_not_in_sources: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the water.
The stadium may look small and distant from the park, at about two kilometres away, if it is visible at all.
The park is likely open to the public without a ticket.

name: Prudential Center
label: Prudential Center
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Championship Plaza' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Championship Plaza' (way/259492793): middle (97 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1421198650: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Prudential Center' (288 m across).
notes: Arena home of the New Jersey Devils.

text.description:
Prudential Center is a large indoor arena in downtown Newark, opened in 2007. It is home to the New Jersey Devils ice hockey team, the New York Sirens and Seton Hall University's men's basketball team, and it also hosts big concerts. Fans and sports writers call it "The Rock", a nod to the Rock of Gibraltar logo of Prudential Financial, which has the naming rights.

It photographs well because the building has a clear look. The red and gray outside is inspired by Newark's bricklaying and railroad past. On the Mulberry Street side, two big cylindrical entrance towers stand out most. The front carries one of the largest LED screens in the world, about 4,800 square feet.

The best easy shot is from Championship Plaza on Mulberry Street, where a 22-foot stainless steel hockey player sculpture makes a strong foreground and the arena rises behind it. Put the figure on one side of the frame and let the building fill the rest, so the picture tells people at once where you are. The arena is big, so a wide shot of the whole building may mean a few steps back along Mulberry or Lafayette Street. For a second picture, try the front entrance, where a statue of Martin Brodeur stands in the foreground. Event days can be busy, so allow a little patience for a clear view.
text.geographic_location: Prudential Center is in downtown Newark, New Jersey. Championship Plaza, the photo spot, is on Mulberry Street between Edison Place and Market Street, right beside the arena.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the centre of downtown Newark and head for the arena by taxi or hired scooter. Championship Plaza is on Mulberry Street, between Edison Place and Market Street, next to the arena. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the sculpture and the arena sit together in one frame. If the building will not fit when you are close to the sculpture, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x). Use the telephoto lens (2x or more) for details such as the entrance towers or the LED screen.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Championship Plaza (Plaza on Mulberry Street between Edison Place and Market Street, near the arena). The 22-foot stainless steel hockey player sculpture in the foreground, with the arena behind it. The arena lies to the south-west of this point. From there, try to include the hockey player sculpture with the arena behind it, and adjust your position as needed.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the sculpture on one third of the frame, with the arena filling the rest. Keep the phone level so the building does not lean. If you want the whole building, take a few steps back along Mulberry or Lafayette Street. For another view, walk to the front entrance and photograph Martin Brodeur's statue with the arena behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sculpture to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out. Stainless steel can glare, so check the highlights on screen. In portrait mode, the sculpture can stand out from the building, but check the edges around the figure.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight makes the red and gray building and the sculpture easy to read. Visit on a day without an event for fewer people in the frame.

text.access_note: The plaza is outside beside the arena. Check the access rules for the arena itself on the official site before you go.

name: Newark Penn Station
label: Newark Penn Station
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/2051677435: the OpenStreetMap point 'Newark Penn Station'.
notes: Historic 1935 Art Deco railway station with a grand waiting room.

text.description:
Newark Penn Station is the city's main rail and bus hub, and it is also one of the better-looking buildings in the centre of Newark. It was designed by McKim, Mead & White, the architects behind the original Penn Station in New York, and it mixes Art Deco and Neo-Classical features. It was dedicated on 23 March 1935, and the south-eastern half was finished in 1937 after the older station was demolished. A big restoration in 2007 cleaned up the facade and the historic interior materials, including the plaster ceilings, marble and limestone.

That gives you two kinds of picture. Outside, the long, formal stone frontage suits a straight-on, symmetrical shot. Inside, the main waiting room has medallions showing the history of transport, from wagons and steamships to cars and aeroplanes, and chandeliers decorated with Zodiac signs. Both are good subjects for a phone, because they are graphic and don't depend on a perfect sky.

The station is busy, so expect people walking through your frame. Use them as scale, or wait a few seconds for a gap. Stay out of the way of commuters, and keep to public areas. Be ready for the building to look flat on a grey day, so look for the carved detail and the lamps rather than the whole front.
text.geographic_location: In central Newark, New Jersey, at Raymond Plaza between Market Street and Raymond Boulevard. It sits beside the Passaic River crossing and is linked by skybridges to nearby office buildings.
text.directions_text: From the centre of Newark, go to Raymond Plaza, or arrive by Amtrak, NJ Transit or PATH, which all serve the station itself. From there the station is about 2 minutes on foot to the south-east. The phone icon on the map is about 140 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the facade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) inside the waiting room or if you are close to the building. Use 2x-5x telephoto for medallions, lamps and carved details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 140 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. The station is in front of you to the south-east. Walk the last couple of minutes if you want a closer, straighter view of the frontage.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the vertical edges of the building up with them, so the stonework doesn't lean. Keep the whole frontage in one frame at 1x, then move closer for details. Inside, shoot upwards to include the ceiling and chandeliers, and use the arched shapes and floor lines to lead the eye.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the facade to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky doesn't wash out. Indoors, hold the phone steady with both hands and let night mode work if it switches on by itself.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on stonework. Mid-morning outside the commuter rush may be calmer inside the building.

text.access_note: The station is a working public transport building, so check the official site before you go for any rules about photography or access to particular areas.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon light is usually softer on stone facades.
The station is busiest at commuter times, so quieter periods may exist outside the rush hour.
Photography in public areas of a working station is generally tolerated, but rules may vary.
A facade can look flat in grey weather.

name: The Newark Museum of Art
label: Newark Museum of Art
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/259617388: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Newark Museum' (149 m across).

text.description: The Newark Museum of Art is New Jersey's largest museum, and it is as interesting to look at from outside as it is inside. It sits on Washington Park and is really a cluster of buildings from different eras. The main building was designed by Jarvis Hunt and opened in the 1920s after a gift from Louis Bamberger. Over the years the museum has grown to the south into a red brick former YMCA, to the north into the 1885 Ballantine House, and to the west into another building. Michael Graves redesigned much of it in 1990. That mix of styles is what makes it rewarding to photograph: you can pick out the different parts and show how they fit together. Behind the museum, the Alice Ransom Dreyfuss Memorial Garden holds contemporary sculpture, a stone schoolhouse dated 1784 and the Newark Fire Museum. Together they make a good second set of pictures, with old and new side by side. The museum is also known for its Tibetan art collection, one of the largest in the Western Hemisphere. Because the whole complex is around 149 m across, you will not fit it into one frame up close. Take a wide shot from a distance first, then move in for details such as entrances, brickwork and sculpture. The front doors were reopened in 2018 with a ramp, so the main entrance is worth a frame of its own.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in central Newark, New Jersey, on the edge of Washington Park. The red brick former YMCA stands to its south and the Ballantine House to its north.
text.directions_text: There is no station or tram stop right at this spot, so head for Washington Park in central Newark, which is the easiest landmark to aim for. Getting there by taxi or hired scooter is the simplest option. Once you are at the park, the museum buildings are along its edge and easy to spot. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the full width of the building, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as doorways, windows and sculpture.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. That is too close to see the whole thing, so walk out to the Washington Park side and turn back to face the building. For the garden, go round behind the museum and shoot back towards the walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the vertical lines of the building straight by lining them up with the grid. Use the 0.5x lens from further back, and keep a patch of park or sky in the frame to give a sense of scale. For the garden, put a sculpture or the 1784 schoolhouse in the foreground and let the museum wall sit behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright so the brick and stone keep their colour. Use portrait mode for close-ups of sculpture, and take a panorama only if you can stand far enough back to keep the lines straight.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear day, ideally mid-morning or later in the afternoon, when the light is softer and the facade is not in harsh midday glare.

text.access_note: The building and its garden are part of a ticketed museum, so check the official site before you go for opening times, entry rules and photography rules inside.
claims_not_in_sources: The whole building is best seen from the Washington Park side, at some distance from the entrance.
Softer light in mid-morning or later in the afternoon suits the facade better than midday sun.
The garden behind the museum can be reached by walking round the building, though access may vary.
At 0.5x, the full width of the complex can be captured from across the park.

name: Branch Brook Park
label: Branch Brook Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Cherry Blossom Welcome Center' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Cherry Blossom Welcome Center' (way/339445462): middle (44 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/411817733: large area 'Branch Brook Park' (5188 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Olmsted-designed park famous for its cherry blossoms.

text.description:
Branch Brook Park is a big, green county park in Newark's North Ward, and in April it turns pink and white. It holds the largest collection of cherry blossom trees in the United States, with more than 5,000 trees in over eighteen varieties. The first trees came from a 1927 gift by Caroline Bamberger Fuld. The park was created in 1895 as the nation's first county park, and at 360 acres it is the largest public park in the city.

For a phone photo, the best-known place is the grove of trees outside the Cherry Blossom Welcome Center. Guides point to it as the place with the highest concentration of blossom trees, so you can frame people standing under the branches in the open air. The blossom fills the frame from a few steps away, which suits a phone well. There is no need for a long view.

Peak bloom is typically the second and third week of April, and the Welcome Center area gets very crowded on festival weekends. If you want a calmer picture, walk to Branch Brook Park Drive at the north end of the park, where the cherry trees grow in smaller clusters. The other classic view is from Prudential Concert Grove, with cherry trees and lawn in front and the Cathedral Basilica of the Sacred Heart behind. Outside the blossom season the park is still a pleasant place for a lakeside walk and some relaxed photos of meadows and trees.
text.geographic_location: Branch Brook Park lies in the North Ward of Newark, between the neighbourhoods of Forest Hill and Roseville. The Cathedral Basilica of the Sacred Heart stands on its east side.
text.directions_text: The main part of the park lies about 1.6 km to the south of it. From the Welcome Center you can wander on to Prudential Concert Grove or Branch Brook Park Drive if you want other views. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the grove and the people under the trees. Switch to the telephoto (2x or more) to pick out a single branch of blossom, and to the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you want the whole canopy overhead.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Cherry Blossom Welcome Center (grove of trees outside the center). A dense grove of pink and white cherry trees framing visitors in the open air beside the Welcome Center. From here the photo shows a dense grove of pink and white cherry trees framing visitors in the open air beside the Welcome Center. The wider park spreads away to the south.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Take a few steps in among the trees and let the branches form a frame around your companions. Turn on gridlines and keep the horizon level. For a different picture, try Prudential Concert Grove, with cherry trees and lawn in front and the Cathedral Basilica of the Sacred Heart behind, or the quieter clusters along Branch Brook Park Drive.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the blossom to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the pale petals keep their detail against a bright sky. Portrait mode works well for close shots of a person with blossom softly blurred behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Peak bloom is typically the second and third week of April, but the Welcome Center is very crowded at weekends during the festival. Go early on a weekday if you can.

text.access_note: Branch Brook Park is a public county park, but festival-time arrangements may vary, so check the official site before you go.

name: Cathedral Basilica of the Sacred Heart (Newark, New Jersey)
label: Cathedral Basilica
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Branch Brook Park' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Branch Brook Park' (way/411817733): edge nearest the subject (5163 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/5506232: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Cathedral Basilica of the Sacred Heart' (168 m across).
notes: Gothic Revival cathedral, one of the largest in the US.

text.description: The Cathedral Basilica of the Sacred Heart is the seat of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Newark and the fifth-largest cathedral in North America. It sits on the edge of Branch Brook Park, and that pairing is what makes it so good for photographs. From the park's edge you can see the west façade and twin towers. The building is roughly the size of Westminster Abbey. Construction began in 1899 and finished in 1954. The design started as an English-Irish Gothic Revival church but was changed to French Gothic Revival. The 36-foot rose window over the main entrance is described as the largest in the Catholic Church in the Western Hemisphere, so it is worth looking for the circular glass on the front. In spring the park's cherry blossom season can give you pink foreground for the towers. For a second view, walk round to the entrance end for the standard street-level shot of the whole front of the building. Keep your phone level and the towers central, and give yourself some sky above them. The main door is reported to be locked, with visitors asked to use the side entrance, so plan your photos outside first and check the official site before you go in.
text.geographic_location: The cathedral basilica is in the Lower Broadway neighbourhood of Newark, New Jersey, facing Branch Brook Park. It stands in the Forest Hill section of the North Ward.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is given for this spot, so plan your own way to the cathedral on the edge of Branch Brook Park. Street parking is the usual option, as there is no dedicated lot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit both towers and some of the park in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the towers and the rose window.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Branch Brook Park (park side of the cathedral, looking back toward the west façade and twin towers). The west façade and twin towers rising above the park's edge, the classic exterior frame for the basilica. For the classic exterior view of the west façade and twin towers, look from the edge of Branch Brook Park.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the towers up with the vertical lines so they do not lean. Leave a little sky above the spires and let the park fill the bottom of the frame. For an alternative, walk to the entrance end for the full front of the building in a straight-on street-level shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the pale stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky does not wash out. Portrait mode is not needed for this building, but you can use it for a family photo in the park with the towers behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, around golden hour, is recommended for the shots from the park's edge. In spring, the cherry blossom season in the park adds colour.

text.access_note: The park is open public space, but the cathedral is a working place of worship, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements and rules; the main door is reported locked, with visitors using the side entrance.
claims_not_in_sources: The ultra-wide lens can make the towers lean inward if you tilt the phone upwards, so keep the phone level.

name: Newark Public Library
label: Newark Public Library
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Harriet Tubman Square' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Harriet Tubman Square' (node/7682101463): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/259617385: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Newark Public Library' (94 m across).

text.description:
The Newark Public Library is the main branch of the city's library system. It stands at 5 Washington Street and opened in 1901. It was designed by Rankin and Kellogg and takes its inspiration from the 15th-century Palazzo Strozzi in Florence, which explains the formal, stone-built look of the front. For a time the building also housed a museum, a lecture hall and a gallery, and the Newark Museum was founded inside it in 1909.

It photographs well because the library faces a public park, Harriet Tubman Square (formerly Washington Park). That open space gives you room to step back and fit the whole Beaux-Arts front into the frame, with the park's greenery as a foreground. From the northern corner of the square you look north-west straight at the facade.

For a phone, this is a simple, rewarding shot. Stand keep the phone level so the vertical lines stay straight, and take one wide frame of the whole building. Then move closer or zoom in for the stonework and entrance details. Look at the sky and the shadows on the facade before you set up.
text.geographic_location: The library is in downtown Newark, New Jersey, on Washington Street, directly across from Harriet Tubman Square (formerly Washington Park).
text.directions_text: No station is listed for this spot, so head for downtown Newark and walk to Washington Street. From there the library is about 120 m to the north-west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full facade from across the park. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if trees or other people force you to stand closer. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the entrance and stone details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Harriet Tubman Square (northern corner of the square, looking northwest at the library facade). The Beaux-Arts front of the Newark Public Library, framed across the open park from its northern corner. From here you look north-west across the open park at the Beaux-Arts front of the library.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the building up with them, so the vertical lines stay straight. Keep the whole facade in frame with a strip of the park in the foreground. Then take a second, tighter shot of the entrance with the telephoto lens.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Hold the phone steady for a moment before each shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Check the light on the day, as shadows and glare on the facade change through the day.

text.access_note: The park is a public square and the library is open to visitors, but check the official site before you go for opening times and any rules on photography inside.

name: Newark City Hall
label: Newark City Hall
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Broad Street' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Broad Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/387208849: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Newark City Hall' (112 m across).
notes: 1906 Beaux-Arts municipal building with a green dome.

text.description: Newark City Hall is a five-storey Beaux Arts building with a golden dome, and the dome is the reason to stop here. It was built in 1902 and added to the National Register of Historic Places on 17 February 1978. The developer Harry Grant paid for the dome to be covered in 24 carat gold in 1986, so it still stands out against the sky and the modern towers behind. The building is large and its columns and stonework are quite detailed. On a phone the trick is to give it room: stand back on the street so the whole facade and the dome fit in one frame, with trees and the taller buildings around it adding scale. The whole front is in view, with the dome above the columns. If you want a different angle, the main entrance steps give a closer view of the facade with the dome rising above. Franklin Street gives a quieter, side-on view. Take the shot in daylight, when the dome shows up best. The George Floyd statue outside is also worth a quick photo while you are there. Keep a little space around the edges of your frame, as a tilted phone can make the columns lean inwards.
text.geographic_location: Newark City Hall is at 920 Broad Street in the Government Center area of Newark, Essex County, New Jersey.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Government Center area of Newark, on Broad Street. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from where you stand, which should fit the whole building and dome. If you cannot step back far enough, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a close-up of the dome and its gold.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Broad Street (sidewalk across from the front facade, standing back from the building). The whole building with its golden dome and columns, framed against the surrounding trees and modern towers. On the pavement across from the front facade, and stay back from the building. City Hall is to the south-east of you. From here the photo shows the whole building with its golden dome and columns, framed by trees and modern towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the columns up with the vertical lines so the building looks straight. Put the dome in the upper third of the frame, with some sky above it. For a different view, try the main entrance steps for a closer look at the facade, or Franklin Street for a side-on view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the dome to focus on it, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the gold keeps its detail against a bright sky. If the ultra-wide makes the edges look stretched, step back and use the default lens (1x).
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime, when the dome is most prominent.

text.access_note: The exterior can be photographed from the public street, but access inside the building may be restricted, so check the official site before you go.

name: Old First Presbyterian Church (Newark, New Jersey)
label: Old First Presbyterian
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Broad Street' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Broad Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/330378211: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'First Presbyterian Church' (75 m across).

text.description:
Old First Presbyterian Church, now known as First Church Newark, stands at 820 Broad Street in the Four Corners Historic District. The building dates from 1787, and the grounds include an old burial ground. Several people who served New Jersey in Congress are buried there, including William Burnet and Silas Condit. The church was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1972.

It photographs well because the front of the church is easy to see straight on from the pavement. Next to it is the Hotel Indigo building, which gives a useful contrast between old and new in the same picture. Stand on the Broad Street sidewalk, look across towards the church and let the whole facade fill the frame. Keep your phone upright so the tower and roofline both fit, and use the gridlines to keep the vertical lines straight. If you cannot fit the whole building in at the default lens (1x), step back a little rather than tilting the phone upwards, which makes the walls lean. Broad Street is busy, so stay on the sidewalk and take care when crossing. Use this street side as your starting point, then try a closer shot of the doorway or the stonework.
text.geographic_location: In central Newark, on the Broad Street side of the Four Corners Historic District, next to the Hotel Indigo building.
text.directions_text: Head for the Four Corners area of central Newark and look for 820 Broad Street. Follow the map from the Four Corners area. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the straight-on view of the facade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if traffic or the pavement stops you stepping back far enough. Use telephoto (2x or more) for details such as the doorway or windows.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Broad Street (sidewalk on the Broad Street side, looking east toward the church; the Wikimedia photo was taken from roughly 40.73428, -74.17264). The church's front and facade as seen straight on from the street, with the neighboring Hotel Indigo building next to it. From here you see the front of the church head-on, with the Hotel Indigo building beside it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the church's vertical edges with them. Keep the phone level and upright, and include a little sky above the roof. Let the hotel building show at one edge to give a sense of the street setting. For a second picture, move closer and use 2x to pick out the entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the church to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky looks washed out. Check the verticals against the gridlines before you press the shutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime in clear weather suits the facade, as the church can be seen clearly then.

text.access_note: The church exterior can be photographed from the public sidewalk; for visits to the grounds, the burial ground or the inside, check the official site before you go.

name: Military Park (Newark)
label: Military Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Wars of America' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Wars of America' (node/4719897387): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/76554678: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Military Park' (402 m across).
notes: Historic downtown park on Broad Street.

text.description: Military Park is a six-acre green space in the middle of downtown Newark, roughly triangular and bordered by Park Place, Rector Street and Broad Street. It was laid out by Robert Treat as a training ground for soldiers and later served as an army campground. For photographs, the main subject is Wars of America, a bronze group of figures and horses on a raised granite base, made by Gutzon Borglum, the sculptor of Mount Rushmore. The statue sits at the head of a long sword shape set into the ground. The sword is about eighty yards long, so the walkway gives you strong leading lines. Behind the statue you get the park's lawns and the downtown towers, which put the old monument in a modern city setting. The park was renovated and reopened in June 2014, so the lawns and paths are tidy. Seasonal outdoor dining, events and a carousel may appear in your frames, so wait a moment for a clear view if you want just the sculpture. Step back and use the sword's lines to draw the eye in, then move close for details of the horses and figures.
text.geographic_location: In downtown Newark, New Jersey, in the park between Park Place, Rector Street and Broad Street. The Wars of America sculpture is in the south-western part of the park, and the middle of the park lies to the north-east of it.
text.directions_text: Head for downtown Newark and the south-western end of Military Park, near Raymond Boulevard and Park Place. A light rail station called Military Park Newark lies under the south-western end of the park, where the monument stands. Once you are in the park, look for the long sword-shaped walkway; the bronze stands at its head. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the bronze and its granite base. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) to catch the whole sword-shaped walkway, then try telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details of the horses and figures.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (stand on the sword-shaped walkway or grass around the bronze, shooting toward its raised granite base). The bronze Borglum group of figures and horses on its granite pedestal, with the park's lawns and downtown towers behind it. Facing the raised granite base. From here the photo shows the bronze group of figures and horses on its pedestal, with the park's lawns and the downtown towers behind. The middle of the park lies to the north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the pedestal on a vertical line, with the towers filling the space above and behind it. Crouch a little so the bronze rises against the sky. For a second view, walk out onto the lawn and take a wide shot across the park towards the tall office towers on its eastern side, including the Military Park Building.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bronze to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the dark metal keeps its detail against the bright sky. Hold the phone level, because the straight edges of the pedestal and towers show any tilt.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: No particular time is recommended. Softer morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters bronze and avoids harsh midday shadows, and quieter times make it easier to get a frame without people.

text.access_note: It is a public city park, but events and seasonal features may change what is open, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Softer morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters bronze and avoids harsh midday shadows.
The park is likely to be quieter at less busy times of day, making clear frames easier.

name: John Ballantine House
label: Ballantine House
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/763164733: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'John Ballantine House' (34 m across).
notes: Gilded Age mansion inside the Newark Museum complex.

text.description:
The John Ballantine House is a Victorian house museum on Washington Street, looking across to Washington Park. It was built in 1884 for John Holme Ballantine and his wife Jeannette Boyd. He was the son of the founder of the Ballantine beer brewery, and he took over as head of the brewery in 1883. The architect was George Edward Harney of New York. When it went up it was one of several grand houses facing the park, and it is now the only one left. That makes it a good place to picture how the area once looked.

It photographs well because the building is so distinctive. The three-storey walls are salmon-coloured pressed brick with sandstone trim, and the front has five uneven bays with a gabled centre section. The entrance sits under a stone portico with rounded arches on granite columns. The warm brick against the greenery of the park makes a simple, balanced picture, and the portico gives you a good close-up. The house was named a National Historic Landmark in 1985. It is owned by The Newark Museum of Art and reopened in November 2023 after a restoration of the outside and inside.

For a phone, the easiest shot is the whole front from across the street, with the park trees at the edge of the frame. Then move in for a second picture of the portico and the brick and stone details. Watch for passing cars and parked vehicles when you line up the wide view.
text.geographic_location: The house is in the Washington Park section of Newark, on the west side of Washington Street at the southern edge of the park. It is owned and managed by The Newark Museum of Art.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Washington Park area of central Newark. The house is at 49 Washington Street, on the west side of the street with the park opposite. Once you are in the park, you only need to look for the salmon-coloured brick house with the stone portico. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the full front from across the street. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close and cannot fit the house in. Use 2x or more for the portico and brick details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. In practice, cross Washington Street towards Washington Park and turn back to face the house. That gives you room for the whole width of the front.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the central gabled bay with the middle vertical line. Keep the phone level so the walls do not lean inwards. Leave a little space for the roof and a strip of park foreground. Then step closer and take a second shot of the portico arches and columns.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brick wall to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright, so the salmon colour stays rich rather than washed out. Take your wide shots with the phone held upright.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, when the front of the house is likely to be lit. Soft, bright overcast days also suit the brick colour.

text.access_note: The house is a museum open for tours, so check the official site before you go; the outside can be photographed from the street and park.

name: Newark Paramount Theatre
label: Paramount Theatre
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Market Street' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Market Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q121754674: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description: The Newark Paramount Theatre is a former vaudeville house that became a film "movie palace" in the Four Corners Historic District of Downtown Newark. It opened in 1886 and closed in 1986. The architect Thomas W. Lamb was brought in to expand and renovate it in the early 20th century, and it took the Paramount name around 1930. Billie Holiday performed here, and Jerry Lewis worked as an usher in his youth. Its facade was also dressed up as the "New Art" cinema in the 2019 film Joker. The theatre is derelict and closed, and its roof collapsed in 2021, so the street-facing front is the only part you can photograph. Redevelopment plans say the historic facade and marquee are to be kept and restored, so the building may look different when you visit. The tall vertical "Paramount" sign and the "Newark" marquee are what make it worth a stop. They give you bold lettering and strong vertical lines, with the street in front for scale. Stand on Market Street, face the front, and keep the sign and marquee together in one frame. Include a little pavement and street at the bottom so the building feels grounded. If the sign is too tall to fit from close up, step back across the road, and watch for passing traffic. Do not try to go inside or climb on any fencing. If you are inside the Prudential Center, a clear view down onto the roofline and signage from its glass-walled concourse is a second option.
text.geographic_location: In the Four Corners Historic District of Downtown Newark, on the Market Street side a short way east of the Market and Broad Street crossing. The Prudential Center arena is nearby.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed close by, so head for the Four Corners area of Downtown Newark. Look for Market Street and the vertical Paramount sign. Check the exact frontage on the map before you go, as the building is also linked to Broad Street. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole facade with the street in front. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is narrow and the sign will not fit, and use 2x or the telephoto lens to pick out the lettering and marquee detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Market Street (in front of the theatre at 195 Market Street, facing the facade). The vertical 'Paramount' sign and the 'Newark' marquee on the front of the former theatre, with the street in the foreground. The theatre is listed at 195 Market Street, though a Broad Street address is also given, so check on the day. The view shows the vertical "Paramount" sign and the "Newark" marquee, with the street in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the vertical sign up with one of the vertical grid lines so the building does not lean. Keep the marquee in the upper half of the frame and a strip of street at the bottom. If you are inside the Prudential Center, the glass-walled concourse gives a higher view of the roofline and signage as an alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sign to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky behind is washing out. Hold the phone upright with both hands, as the sign is tall and wobble shows in the lettering.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight is the safest choice, because the sign and marquee read clearly and you can see the street around you. Pick a quieter moment if you want fewer cars and passers-by in the frame.

text.access_note: The theatre is closed and derelict, with no public access inside, so photograph the facade from the public street and check local notices before you go.

name: Seated Lincoln (Borglum)
label: Seated Lincoln
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Essex County Courthouse Plaza' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Essex County Courthouse' (pois); moved 20 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/4719982114: the OpenStreetMap point 'Seated Lincoln'.
notes: Gutzon Borglum's bronze of Lincoln outside the courthouse.

text.description:
This is a larger-than-life bronze of Abraham Lincoln, made by Gutzon Borglum and unveiled in 1911. Instead of standing on a tall plinth, Lincoln sits at one end of a bronze bench with his stovepipe hat beside him. Borglum took the idea from accounts of Lincoln sitting alone on a bench to think during the Civil War. At the unveiling, Theodore Roosevelt is said to have remarked that it didn't look like a monument at all. The statue was paid for by a bequest from Newark businessman Amos Hoagland Van Horn, and it sits on a low stone platform beside the steps of the Essex County Courthouse.

It photographs well because it is informal and friendly, and the courthouse gives it a strong backdrop. For a different feel, walk to the statue and take a close, eye-level frame of the face, the bench and the hat. The corner of Market Street and Springfield Avenue gives a street-level view with the downtown side of Market Street behind him. Take a quick look at the current layout when you arrive, as street furniture and fencing can change.
text.geographic_location: In downtown Newark, New Jersey, beside the steps of the Essex County Courthouse. The Market Street and Springfield Avenue corner is a nearby intersection.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Essex County Courthouse in downtown Newark, on foot or by car. From there the statue is about 1 minute on foot to the south-east, beside the courthouse steps. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the wide view of statue and courthouse together. Switch to the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a tighter frame of Lincoln's face. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you stand close and want the whole bench and steps in the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Essex County Courthouse Plaza (front, facing west toward the statue). The seated bronze Lincoln in the foreground with the Essex County Courthouse behind him. From here you get the seated bronze Lincoln in the foreground with the Essex County Courthouse behind him, which is the standard composition for this sculpture.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put Lincoln on one third line, leaving the courthouse in the rest of the frame. Hold the phone at chest height so the statue is not distorted. As an alternative, try the Market Street and Springfield Avenue corner for a street-level view. For a close, eye-level shot, sit on the bench next to him and photograph the hat and the bench.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bronze to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the bright sky behind is washing out the statue. Bronze looks best slightly darker. Portrait mode can work for the close shot, but check that the edges of the figure stay clean.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft daylight, such as morning or late afternoon, usually suits bronze better than harsh midday sun. Early in the day there are also likely to be fewer people around the courthouse steps.

text.access_note: The statue stands beside the courthouse steps; check the official site before you go in case there are any access or security restrictions around the courthouse.

name: Indian and the Puritan
label: Indian and the Puritan
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Washington Park' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Washington Park' (node/2650516435): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/4721829028: the OpenStreetMap point 'Indian and the Puritan'.
notes: Gutzon Borglum sculpture near Newark's courthouse area.

text.description:
Indian and the Puritan is a monument made in 1916 by Gutzon Borglum, the sculptor of Mount Rushmore. A tall bronze lamp standard, about 22 feet (6.7 m) high, rises above two carved marble figures, a Native American and a Puritan. Newark's city seal and two inscriptions about the city's history are on the standard. The city commissioned it for its 250th anniversary, which covered 1666 to 1916. It was moved to its present area in 1977, and it has been on the National Register of Historic Places since 1994.

It photographs well because it is a real piece of street sculpture. You get the dark bronze, the pale marble and the city's commercial and cultural buildings behind. From there you look north-east and the statue sits in the park with downtown Newark rising behind it. The exact spot where the monument stands can vary slightly, so check on the day and look for it on the ground when you arrive. The marble figures show some wear and vandalism, so a closer shot of the full lamp standard against the surrounding streets is a good second picture. Take a wide view first, then move in for a tighter one of the figures.
text.geographic_location: In downtown Newark, in Harriet Tubman Square (formerly Washington Park), opposite the Newark Public Library at 5 Washington Street.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Newark Public Library on Washington Street in downtown Newark. The monument is opposite the library. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the statue with the city behind it. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close and need the whole 22-foot standard. Use 2x or the telephoto to fill the frame with the marble figures.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Washington Park (north end of the park, where the monument now stands). The statue set in the park with downtown Newark's commercial and cultural buildings behind it. For a second view, walk up to the monument itself and shoot the full bronze lamp standard with the Puritan and Indian figures at its base, framed by the streets around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the lamp standard on one vertical line so it stands upright. Keep the base of the figures in the frame and let the buildings fill the background. When you walk up close, tilt the phone up slowly and check that the standard does not lean. Take one wide shot and one tighter shot of the figures.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the marble figures to set focus and exposure, then lower the exposure slider a little if the bright sky is making the bronze too dark. Portrait mode is not needed for a statue, so keep it in normal photo mode.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kinder to the marble and bronze than harsh midday sun. Early on a weekday is likely to be quieter.

text.access_note: The park is an open public space, but check the official site or the signs on the ground before you go in case anything has changed.

name: Trinity & St. Philip's Cathedral (Newark, New Jersey)
label: Trinity & St. Philip's
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Military Park' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Military Park' (way/76554678): middle (401 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/310455960: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Trinity and St. Philip's Cathedral' (51 m across).

text.description: Trinity & St. Philip's Cathedral stands at the corner of Broad and Rector Streets, at the northern end of Military Park in central Newark. It photographs well because the park gives you open ground in front of it. You can step back far enough to fit the front and the tower into one frame, with lawns and paths leading the eye towards the building. The church dates from 1810, built to replace an earlier stone church of 1743 that was damaged in the American Revolutionary War. A chancel and sanctuary were added at the east end in 1857. It became a cathedral in 1944 and is the seat of the Episcopal Diocese of Newark. In 1992 the name 'St. Philip's' was added, recalling St. Philip's, a parish on High and West Market Streets whose church burned in 1964 and which merged with Trinity two years later. The building is on the National Register of Historic Places and is part of the Military Park Commons Historic District. For a phone photo, start from the park, facing the cathedral, and let a path or a stretch of lawn fill the lower part of the picture. Then walk up to the corner of Broad Street and Rector Street for a second, street-level view of the front and its historic marker. Keep your phone upright for the tower and turn it sideways for the whole front.
text.geographic_location: In central Newark, at the corner of Broad Street and Rector Street, at the northern end of Military Park. The cathedral's address is 608 Broad Street.
text.directions_text: Head for Military Park in central Newark, by taxi if you are coming from further away. Once in the park, the cathedral is to the north, at the top end of the park. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the cathedral with the park in front of it. Switch to telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the tower and front details. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only from the street corner, where you are close to the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Military Park (north end of the park, facing the cathedral). The cathedral's front and tower at the north end of the triangular park, with the park's lawns and paths in the foreground. From here the photo shows the cathedral's front and tower at the end of the triangular park, with lawns and paths in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the tower on one of the vertical lines, with a path leading towards it. Keep the phone level so the tower doesn't lean. As an alternative, go to the corner of Broad Street and Rector Street for a street-level view of the front and its historic marker.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the cathedral's front to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Ultra-wide close to the building can stretch the edges and make the tower lean, so step back and use 1x or 2x where you can.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters stonework, and early in the day there are likely to be fewer people in the park.

text.access_note: The park and the street corner are open public space for outside photos; if you want to photograph inside the cathedral, check the official site before you go.
